connector: Harriet is fifteen now, and stronger than most of the men in the fields. Working on a farm near home, she meets Jim, who has run away twice and plans to go again. He tells her about trains. Listen carefully for which trains he means, and watch what Harriet decides when the moment comes.

a.raw: harriet listened to the exciting stories her heart pounded with new hope
a.fixed: Harriet listened to the exciting stories. Her heart pounded with new hope.
a.why: Capital H on Harriet; the adjective exciting describes the stories; a period ends the first sentence; capital H to start the second sentence; the adjective new describes the hope.

b.raw: jim told stories about the busy city harriet listened to every word
b.fixed: Jim told stories about the busy city. Harriet listened to every word.
b.why: Capital J on the name Jim; the adjective busy describes the city; a period ends the first sentence; capital H on Harriet starts the second one.

fill1.h1: When you leave a room, you go ___ of it. Which part means out?
fill1.why: ex- means out: ex + it = to go out.

fill2.h1: A balloon getting bigger pushes outward on every side. Which part means out?
fill2.why: ex- means out: ex + pand = to stretch out, to get bigger.

fill3.h1: Putting something off means doing it later, after now. Which part means after?
fill3.why: post- means after: post + pone = to put off until later.

fill4.h1: This is the time that comes once a war is over. Which part means after?
fill4.why: post- means after: post + war = after the war.

notes.wgrd: A central idea is only worth saying if you can back it up. State it in one sentence, find two details that prove it, and if they don’t fit, change the idea, not the facts.
vocab: A large farm where one crop is grown (in the South, often using slave labor).
A true book about someone’s life, written by another person.
To stretch out or reach further.
To put off until a later time.
notes.wordParts: ex- means “out of” or “former,” and post- means “after”: exit, extend, postpone, postscript.
notes.grammar: An adjective describes a noun. It is worth adding only if it tells the reader something new: a cold spring tells the season. Cut adjectives that could describe almost anything.
notes.spelling: To split a long name, find the vowels, split between the consonants, and read each chunk. Names follow the same rules as any other word: Bal·ti·more.

transcripts.welcome: Welcome back. Harriet is fifteen now, and very strong. In Chapter 4 she meets someone who has already run away, and she starts hearing about trains, the real kind and another kind. Today you’ll warm up, review the week’s words, read Chapter 4, and plan where you’ll look for research answers. Today’s question: what does a train mean to Harriet?
transcripts.wgrd: A central idea is only worth saying if you can back it up. So today, say it first, in one sentence of your own. Then go hunting for two details that prove it. And here’s the honest part: if your details don’t fit your idea, change the idea, not the facts.
transcripts.dol: The model is a short sentence with two names in it. The sentence to fix runs two thoughts together with nothing between them, and it doesn’t start with a capital. Find the spot where one thought stops. Give the second thought its own beginning, and check every name.
transcripts.guide1: This is the review lesson, so the word work asks you to be the editor. Some describing words in today’s sentences are doing real work, and some are empty. Some of the names are split in the wrong places. Your job is to fix what’s broken, and leave alone what’s already right.
transcripts.morphology: A review of both word parts. You’ve seen some of these words this week, and some only once. Read each meaning, decide between going out and coming after, and type the front. If you get them all on the first try, you really do know these two parts.
transcripts.vocabulary: A last look at this week’s four words. Here’s a challenge: use two of them in the same sentence about Harriet’s life. It’s harder than it sounds, and it’s the best way to find out whether a word is really yours.
transcripts.grammar: Editors cut as often as they add. Look for describing words that tell the reader nothing new, the kind that could describe almost anything. Tap the empty ones. Then think about which word could take that place and really earn it.
transcripts.spelling: It’s the proofreader’s turn. Some of these names are split correctly, and some aren’t. Don’t touch the right ones. Say each one slowly, beat by beat, and only tap a word when its dots don’t match the way you really say it.
transcripts.guide2: Today’s Freedom Watch is about hearing. Before anyone can go somewhere new, they have to hear that it’s there. Listen for the stories Harriet hears in this chapter, and who tells them. Notice what happens inside her when she hears them, even though she doesn’t say a word.
transcripts.read: In Chapter 4, Harriet meets Jim, who has already tried to run away twice. Listen to his stories about the steam train, and about another railroad with very unusual conductors. Watch for the song the workers sing in the barn. The chapter ends suddenly, with a hard choice. Watch what Harriet decides.
transcripts.guide3: Now you write. The questions ask what Jim tells Harriet about the real train, what the Underground Railroad was, and what the chapter is mostly about. Use the chapter’s own words when you explain the railroad. Then you’ll plan three places to look for your research answers.
transcripts.chapter: The last question asks how the idea of a train changes in this chapter. One train runs on rails. The other doesn’t run on rails at all. Put your central idea in one sentence first. Then find one detail about each train that supports it.
transcripts.workshop: A research plan names real places to look. Not just, I’ll look it up, but which book, which website, and which person. And for each one, what you hope to find there. Today, plan three sources. Next week you’ll start using them.

wordgame.voice: Tap a word part, then the word it finishes. Or drag the part onto the word. Ask what each word is about: going out, or coming after?

why.t: In Chapter 2, Harriet’s mother, Old Rit, saves scraps of cloth from the Big House and sews them, late at night by the fire, into a patchwork quilt of green and brown and yellow. It is the family’s only treasure. ex- means out, and post- means after. Each right word sews one patch into the quilt. Four each lesson, until the quilt is finished.

wordgame.winDay: Four more patches are sewn in. The next lesson’s words add more.
wordgame.win: The quilt is finished, and a North Star is stitched across its middle. ex- = out, post- = after.

songs.title: The Gospel Train
lines: I hear it just at hand.
There’s room for many a more.
songs.heard: A church song about a train that carries good people to heaven.
songs.meant: When Jim sang it in the barn, Harriet knew which train he was thinking about: the Underground Railroad, and his own escape.
songs.q: Jim has just told Harriet about the Underground Railroad. Why would he sing about a train instead of saying his plan out loud?
songs.a: Anyone could be listening. A church song was safe to sing, and only someone who already knew his plan would understand it.

ft.songsIntro: In Chapter 4, Jim tells Harriet about two kinds of railroad. Then, in the barn, he sings about a third train.
